source.title: Towards Vector Optimization on Low-Dimensional Vector Symbolic Architecture
source.authors: Shijin Duan; Yejia Liu; Gao-Wen Liu; R. Kompella; Shaolei Ren; Xiao-Lin Xu

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares batch-normalized and unnormalized binary VSA/BNN training and reports training-optimization and accuracy outcomes, but does not use the conventional network recipes or the training-speed measure specified in V6.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for batch normalization on binary VSA and BNN models. It does not evaluate the CIFAR training-error claims, shortcut/depth claims, initialization claims, or learning-rate stability claims. Its final-accuracy comparisons do not by themselves measure how quickly accuracy is gained.
record.test_reason: The study measures final inference accuracy, gradient distributions and weight oscillation in binary VSA/BNN training. These are related to V6, but do not establish faster accuracy gains or higher learning-rate tolerance. Its own results do not test V1–V5. Correct the record's tests/T2 classification and V6 tested_not_extracted status.
record.authors_conclusion: The record largely captures the authors' conclusion: BN and KD benefit low-dimensional VSA optimization and inference accuracy, with supporting BNN accuracy comparisons. They argue that BN can become inference thresholds without additional computation, although storing those thresholds adds memory. They also conclude that KD helps confidence calibration; the results more specifically show temperature-dependent confidence changes, including increased confidence on incorrect predictions, rather than demonstrating uniformly improved calibration.
record.recipe_differences: Studies low-dimensional binary VSA and selected binary neural networks, with batch normalization and knowledge distillation; it does not reproduce the conventional network training comparisons in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Vector dimension changes the reported accuracy and variance; teacher capacity and distillation temperature also change some outcomes, but are outside the BN comparison in V6.

fits_no_version.finding: On FashionMNIST at D=64 after 10 epochs, adding encoding-layer BN reduces the reported zero-gradient fraction from 78.13% to 40.63% and the gradient range from approximately ±0.8 to ±0.3. Weight-distribution snapshots through 50 epochs are interpreted as showing less oscillation with BN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Encoding-layer BN makes gradients more active and moderate and reduces weight oscillation in the tested binary LDC training recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 2 reports higher final FashionMNIST inference accuracy with BN at every tested dimension: 84.24% versus 81.20% at D=32, through 88.53% versus 86.97% at D=1024. At D=1024, across-run standard deviation is 0.17 versus 0.82 percentage points. Across-run variability alone does not measure oscillation during training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: BN improves final inference accuracy across the tested LDC dimensions and reduces across-run accuracy variability at large dimensions.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 16 reports final FashionMNIST accuracy improvements from Binary to Binary+BN: MLP 87.20% to 88.45%, CNN 83.67% to 84.59%, and ResNet-18 91.31% to 91.96%. No training-speed comparison is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: BN improves final inference accuracy in the tested binary MLP, CNN and ResNet-18 models.

record.problems: The study reports final inference accuracy rather than an accuracy-versus-training-time comparison, so it cannot establish faster accuracy gains. The main BN comparisons are on FashionMNIST and low-dimensional binary VSA/BNN models, not CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 conventional networks. Table 16 is a quick validation; no uncertainty is stated there.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were extracted because the reported accuracy comparisons do not measure the training-speed outcome named in V6, and the paper does not test the other versions. These findings are summarized under fits_no_version.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including random or corrupted labels and model-size or regularization conditions.
Spurious local minima and the effect of extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Training-error degradation with depth, identity-shortcut comparisons and the stated initialization exceptions.
Initialization comparisons measuring training speed or trainable depth.
Recovery above the initial stability limit, curvature dynamics, edge-of-stability training and divergence.
Faster accuracy gains and higher learning-rate tolerance with BN versus the same networks without BN; equally fast and stable training using Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: There are no extracted rows to fix. The declared omissions cover the final-accuracy comparisons; no missing result establishes a claim version. Smoother convergence, more active gradients and higher final accuracy do not by themselves establish the training-speed outcome in V6.

versions.untested_parts: Training error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including corrupted or random labels; model size, early stopping and regularization conditions.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual network depth comparisons, and training very deep plain tanh or unnormalized residual networks.
Activation-matched, orthogonal and Gaussian initialization comparisons and trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability limits, loss rise and recovery, sharpness dynamics, and divergence.

The reported final-accuracy and optimization findings concern low-dimensional binary VSA/BNN models. The paper does not measure accuracy gain speed or higher learning-rate tolerance against the same models without BN; those specific V6 outcomes cannot be determined from its reported comparisons.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
